news_drafts.headline: Luton forecasts £2.83m overspend on £54.39m high needs budget for 2026/27
news_drafts.lead:
Luton Council's special educational needs budget is forecast to overspend by £2.83m in 2026/27, according to the first quarterly budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) for the year. The report went to the council's Scrutiny Finance Review Group on 26 October 2026.

All of it falls in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The allocation is £54.39m. The forecast already takes account of £0.88m moved into high needs from the Schools Block, a separate part of the schools grant, a transfer approved in January 2026.

The report says the forecast "continues to be driven by demand-led pressures". It also describes it as "subject to significant uncertainty". It says national SEND reforms have led to a "substantial increase" in requests for Education, Health and Care Needs Assessments, which are assessments of a child's needs for support. The report says these are expected to put further pressure on high needs and on related services paid for from the council's main General Fund budget.

news_drafts.headline: Luton procurement exemptions reach 680 in 2025/26, up from 321 in 2023/24, mostly children's services
news_drafts.lead:
Requests to bypass Luton Council's normal buying rules (exemptions to standing orders) rose to 680 in 2025/26, from 321 in 2023/24 and 566 the year before, the Audit & Governance Committee is told in its annual procurement report. The council approved 471 of them, with £41.8m in approved value.

Children, Families & Education accounted for 311 of the requests, 46% of the total. Its requests were worth £40.6m, 57% by value, and the council approved 244 of them (78%) and £21.4m of the value (53%). The report attributes the increase largely to residential care and foster care placements, out-of-borough school places for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), and home-to-school transport. Rejections also rose, to 209 from 119 in 2023/24. About 44% were for administrative errors and 17% for missing conflict-of-interest declarations.

The council has set up a Passenger Transport Services Framework, a compliant route for buying home-to-school transport, which accounted for about £2.6m of exemption value in 2025/26. The paper says this is expected to "significantly reduce" future requests in that area. Members are asked to acknowledge that the council's processes, commissioning arrangements and procurement policies need further review for residential care, foster care and out-of-borough school placements.

The committee also has the first-quarter budget monitoring (the in-year check of spending against budget). Adult social care is forecasting a £1.7m overspend from demand and complexity, and the High Needs Block, the part of school funding for children with SEND, a £2.8m overspend even after an approved £880k transfer from the Schools Block. The corporate risks paper says the council balanced its 2026/27 budget without using reserves, helped by a 5% council tax rise and the government funding settlement, after a significant 2025/26 deficit that it did not size. It is pursuing a deficit recovery plan over two years.

On internal audit, of 349 recommendations followed up, 76% were fully implemented, 20% were in progress and 4% not yet started.

news_drafts.headline: Luton complaints handling falls short of 80% target despite quarterly improvement
news_drafts.lead: Luton's complaints performance reached 62.4% in-service-level agreement (in-SLA) in the year to March 2026, falling 17.6 percentage points short of the 80% target the council set for the first time in January. The council showed quarterly progress, rising from 60.8% in the first quarter to 65.5% in the fourth, and ombudsman compensation claims dropped 69% to £4,750. However, Children, Family & Education — the highest-risk area — saw complaints surge 54% to 216 while performance remained flat at 34.3% in-SLA, leaving cases unresolved at an average of 52.9 days against an 80% target. The council has committed to a dedicated recovery plan with weekly leadership review and targets of 60% in-SLA by the end of the second quarter and 75% by year-end, conditional on training completion and new platform implementation.

findings.headline: Treasury investments returned an average annualised 3.82% in the six months to 30 September 2026, 9 basis points above the average SONIA of 3.73%.
findings.detail: Treasury investments rose from £18.67 million at 31 March 2026 to £44.92 million at 30 September 2026, of which £32.10 million was Council money and £12.82 million schools money. All were held in Money Market Funds, and the paper reports no approved counterparty or investment limits breached.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing cash returns against SONIA can use the figure directly, and the rise in invested balances is relevant to liquidity planning.
findings.figures: Average annualised return 3.82%; 6-month average SONIA 3.73%; outperformance 0.09% (9 basis points); treasury investments £44.92 million (31 March 2026: £18.67 million); investment income £0.85 million
findings.quote: 9 basis points above average SONIA of 3.73% over the same period.

findings.headline: Recent short-term borrowing has been at around 5.0% to 5.7%, against a Money Market Fund return of approximately 3.8% at 30 September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says borrowing costs have increased and that Treasury will assess the balance between local authority borrowing and PWLB options. It says Bank Rate rose to 4.00% in November 2026, and the Bank of England expects CPI inflation to rise to around 5% by mid-2027.
findings.matters: The gap between the rate on short-term borrowing and the return on cash is the cost of the current funding model, and a finance director or lender would compare it with their own refinancing exposure.
findings.figures: Recent short-term borrowing around 5.0% to 5.7%; Money Market Fund returns approximately 3.8% (30 September 2026); Bank Rate 4.00% (November 2026)
findings.quote: While this retains flexibility, borrowing costs have increased, with recent short -term borrowing at around 5.0% -5.7%.

findings.headline: Non-treasury investments increased by £9.5 million, from £647.9 million at 31 March 2026 to £657.4 million at 30 September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says the movement is mainly a £12.0 million increase in FHL share capital, partly offset by a £2.5 million reduction in FHL loans. Full-year net return is forecast at £32.7 million (5.0%), with part of the six-month income still awaiting confirmation. The paper notes continuing exposure to subsidiary performance, loan recoverability and property income.
findings.matters: Equity and loans to subsidiaries and property are a growing share of the council's exposure, and a finance director or lender would weigh them alongside treasury risk.
findings.figures: Non-treasury investments £657.4 million (31 March 2026: £647.9 million); increase £9.5 million; FHL share capital increase £12.0 million; FHL loans reduction £2.5 million; LLAL loans £507.1 million; forecast net return £32.7 million (5.0%)
findings.quote: Non-treasury investments increased by £9.5 million, from £647.9 million at 31 March 2026 to £657.4 million at 30 September 2026.

findings.headline: Commercial activities are forecast to generate income of £47.9 million in 2026/27, against interest and MRP costs of £14.4 million, a net financing contribution of £33.5 million.
findings.detail: The paper says the net contribution depends on the continued performance of the underlying commercial income streams. The Commercial affordability ratio is forecast at -10.8%, against -13.5% in the original estimate, and the paper attributes this mainly to the higher revised net revenue stream.
findings.matters: A council whose budget depends on a commercial net financing contribution gives a finance director elsewhere, and a lender, a specific income figure to test against the commercial portfolio's performance.
findings.figures: Commercial income forecast £47.9 million (original £48.6 million); interest and MRP £14.4 million; net financing contribution £33.5 million; Commercial ratio -10.8% (original -13.5%)
findings.quote: Commercial activities are forecast to generate income of £47.9 million against associated interest and MRP costs of £14.4 million

findings.headline: Capital expenditure is forecast at £186 million for 2026/27, £21 million above the original estimate, with £52 million, approximately 28%, incurred by 30 September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says the revised financing raises the borrowing requirement from £91 million to £103 million. It says £32 million of that requirement had arisen by 30 September, and the rest depends on delivery in the second half of the year, which creates uncertainty over the timing of external borrowing.
findings.matters: Spending weighted to the second half of the year makes the timing of borrowing uncertain, which affects the refinancing and rate exposure a finance director or lender would assess.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure forecast £186 million (original £165 million); incurred to 30 September £52 million (about 28%); borrowing requirement forecast £103 million (original £91 million); borrowing arisen to 30 September £32 million
findings.quote: Capital expenditure is forecast at £186 million for 2026/27, an increase of £21 million against the original estimate.

daily_post.headline: HRA forecast underspend of £0.301m at Quarter 2, with external income £0.805m above budget and a £0.705m Responsive Repairs pressure.
daily_post.lead: Lower Right to Buy sales are increasing rental income, and rising repairs costs are the trade-off, which is a balance peers managing HRA stock will recognise.
